description: Hi. We're from the University of Indonesia!
summary: Landy is an interactive web app for calculating and determining the feasibility of a given point on the lunar surface as a landing site.
details:
How does it work?

The app uses a set of parameters to process the albedo, roughness, slope, and shade of the lunar surface to calculate the scores given to the user after they've selected a point.

Each point gives information about:

  • Solar illumination angles
  • Direct-to-Earth communication angles
  • Terrain hazard scores
  • Time until sunset (based on the given time calculation date)

The main interface of Landy is the 3D view of the Moon, dubbed the cockpit. This is the screen where the user is able to pinpoint a location on the lunar surface for the app to process and calculate. The 3D view of the Moon is interactive, as the user is able to drag and zoom into any particular point, see historical landing sites and points of interest, and view the projected trajectory of the Sun and the Earth relative to the celestial body. The user may switch to a 2D view of the lunar surface if so desired. The app also displays a Sky dome view for a quick visualization of the Sun based on the perspective of the point and a manual target selector for precise point input.

In addition to the cockpit, there are two other screens that may be used by the user. The scanner, and the matrix.

The scanner is a dynamic list of named potential landing sites that may be filtered using configurable slope and roughness tolerances set by the user. Once a particular site is determined, the user is able to click the "Select as Target Fix & Return" button to quickly go back to the cockpit for the direct visualization of the site.

The matrix is a table of sites ranked using configurable data by the user. The matrix is substantially more comprehensive and detailed, allowing advanced users to filter and select landing sites more easily.

What's in our thought?

The challenge description for Lunar Landing Site Navigator explicitly stated that previous tools for determining lunar landing sites "are built for detailed analysis and are often difficult for non-specialists to use effectively for rapid scenario comparison." As such, our primary concern for the development of the app was usability, interface friendliness, and rapid scenario comparisons.

A lot of enterprise, academic, or otherwise uncommon commercial tools and applications often present themselves with an unfriendly interface that only longtime users of these tools and apps are able to operate correctly and efficiently, not counting the possibility of misreading or misinterpreting the outputs and values of these tools and apps without prior trained experience. We sought to solve that problem by introducing a comfortable interface with descriptive indicators and familiar layouts more suitable for general use.

We also prioritized performance, as we are aware that this app might be used for recreational and educational purposes, and such, must be optimized for general use as well.

What did we use?

We used a web-based stack of React for interactivity, Vite as the build system, Python as the backend server, FastAPI as the server infrastructure, Skyfield as the calculator, and Firebase as the backend host.

The web packages we used are:

  • react
  • react-dom
  • vite
  • vite-plugin-minify
  • oxlint
  • babel-plugin-react-compiler
  • oxc-minify
  • oxc-transform-react
  • oxlint-tsgolint
  • typescript

The Python packages we used are:

  • skyfield
  • flask
  • numpy
  • pydantic

We used SI/AI as the driver for writing code, programming the frontend and the backend of the app, debugging and designing the backend calculation infrastructure, and issue troubleshooter.
